title: [Microsoft Azure] Introducing Azure Catalyst agentic modernization and new AI infrastructure innovations
summary: The top announcements: AKS and Microsoft Foundry Azure Catalyst Windows Server 2028 As AI continues to reshape how every business builds, operates, and competes, it is rapidly emerging as the defining workload in the cloud. This new class of agents, more demanding, complex, and dynamic than anything before them, is rewriting the rules of cloud infrastructure. Reasoning across multi-agent systems, drawing on rich context, acting in real time, and running continuously, they ask more of every layer of the platform beneath them. This week, we’re introducing innovations across Microsoft Azure that set a new standard for how the cloud powers AI: expanded AI core capabilities in Azure to build what’s next, and Azure Catalyst, an intelligent agent-led solution to modernize the apps, data, and infrastructure that already run the business. For years, we have been reengineering every layer of Azure for the unique demands of AI and proving it on the world’s most advanced AI workloads, from leading frontier models to our own GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Teams, and Microsoft 365. That work has forged Azure into a single, co-engineered system, with models, silicon, and cloud infrastructure tuned as one and value compounding at every layer. This week, we take that even further. Explore Azure Catalyst New capabilities across isolated execution, agent networking, context management, and inference efficiency deliver faster, more secure agents with better unit economics. Every innovation rests on an open foundation, giving customers the freedom to run open models and open systems everywhere they operate. There is a wave of new AI applications scaling in production, and years of existing apps and data are moving to the cloud, becoming AI-ready. Azure was built for this moment. Of everything we’re announcing this week, three areas matter most: Building the next generation of AI applications. Silicon, compute, storage, and networking work as one system across Azure for inference, training, and agents. A new connected path from Microsoft Foundry to Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) gives you choice in how and where you run AI. Modernizing apps and data with agents. Azure Catalyst uses AI agents to modernize applications, data, and infrastructure in a fraction of the time and cost of traditional methods, turning decades of technical debt into the fastest path to AI. Extending AI wherever you operate. Azure Local, flex nodes for AKS and Microsoft Foundry extend AI across cloud and distributed environments, governed through Azure Arc. Windows Server 2028, now in public preview, and Windows PCs, bring AI closer to applications, data, and users, providing the choice to meet workload-specific data, performance, regulatory, and cost needs. Build and run the next generation of AI applications Microsoft Foundry and AKS are at the center of how you build and run AI from Foundry’s managed experience, to the deep customization of AKS across models, runtimes, performance, security, and infrastructure. The connected path between them runs from building AI applications and agents to running them at scale. Open-weight models and agents move seamlessly from Foundry to AKS clusters, deployed from cloud to edge, with consistent infrastructure, security policies, and governance. Learn more about Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) Underneath these experiences, AI applications are challenging infrastructure in new ways: writing and executing code autonomously, connecting dynamically to multiple agents, models, tools, and data, and carrying context across long-running tasks. We’re advancing the infrastructure to meet each of these demands: Isolation and confidentiality. With the Agent Sandbox extension for AKS, agent-generated code runs in secure, managed sandboxes with virtual machine (VM)-level isolation for every session, pre-warmed pools for fast startup, and a serverless option with no infrastructure to manage. Azure confidential computing extends protection to sensitive data and workloads while in use. Agent networking and security. With Agent Grid, agents securely connect to other agents, models, tools, data, and Azure services through authenticated, encrypted connections. Identity-driven policies and default-deny network isolation control how agents communicate and what resources they can access. Context and state. Long-context, long-running agents reuse processed prompt context instead of recomputing it on the GPU, so long tasks run faster and cost less. That cached context stays durable and controlled, by you, in your Azure tenant. And we’re making Azure itself more intelligent, building in new workload-aware capabilities that combine deep context for what each AI application requires with what only the platform delivers: GPU and VM performance, topology, and real-time availability across the fleet. AKS AI Manager translates what each model needs into the right infrastructure, placing each deployment where the fleet has the GPU capacity to serve it best. The result is a cloud that makes every AI workload perform better, with faster responses, better economics, and optimal placement decisions. And across all of this, we’re extending our commitment to open-source, giving you transparency and access to the best innovation shaped by the community. Kubernetes, vLLM, and Ray, together with flex nodes for AKS in preview, bring greater flexibility from development through production, including supported GPU environments beyond Azure. You have the freedom to build on the best model, use the right framework, and run where your business needs it. We’re already seeing what’s possible with these innovations. Rockwell Automation is using AI in its factories to help engineers diagnose equipment issues and investigate product failures. As these applications move into production, Rockwell wants to build on what works and bring those approaches to other facilities: Running our factory-level AI applications on Azure gives us one foundation for different AI workloads in production. When something works in one plant, we can adapt it for the next instead of starting over. —Justin Litherland, Vice President, Enterprise Program Management, IT, Rockwell Automation Within our own teams, Microsoft 365 engineering built COSMIC, a shared platform on AKS, to help them ship faster with built-in security, compliance, and reliability. Making infrastructure easier to run matters for developers. COSMIC handles infrastructure centrally so developers can focus on customer experiences rather than Kubernetes operations. What we learn as our own customer continues to shape future Azure capabilities for you. To go deeper at Microsoft Ignite, check out these on-demand sessions: BRK420: Deploy and run Microsoft Foundry models and agents on Kubernetes BRK448: Run secure agent loops in production with isolated sandboxes at scale BRK429: The evolution of Azure infrastructure for AI models, apps, and agents Learn more about Microsoft Foundry Modernize applications and data with Azure Catalyst The need to modernize is universal. But with developers stretched thin, custom code and deep running dependencies, progress often stalls and the backlog keeps growing. Decades of technical debt adds security exposure, cost and complexity, while disconnected tools create friction from assessment to execution. Agents in Azure Catalyst change that, analyzing legacy code, mapping dependencies, and planning and executing with precision. Work that once took months or years can now be done in weeks or even days, even with limited resources and skills, making it possible to modernize systems that were previously out of reach. Learn more about Azure Catalyst The results are real: 1.4 million applications modernized, with businesses like Levi Strauss modernizing its enterprise systems and deploying more than 1,000 agents across them. Azure Catalyst modernizes end to end—across applications, data, and infrastructure in one solution—delivered in the tools hundreds of millions of developers and IT professionals already use. Here’s what sets it apart: One connected experience Azure Catalyst connects IT teams and developers across an end-to-end process from discovery to design and execution. New capabilities add rich estate insights, AI-powered application discovery, modernization strategy and cost comparisons, and AI-generated migration waves. Execution spans applications, containers, storage, networking, and databases, and builds on existing coverage for Java and .NET modernization and migration support for VMware, Hyper-V, and physical servers. Tailored to your business Governance rulebooks and bring-your-own-model support let you set the standards, guardrails, and models agents follow, so plans fit your architecture, priorities, and security requirements. Reusable runbooks and skills make what works repeatable, so every project meets your exact standards. Secure from the start Outdated applications and data increase security exposure. Azure Catalyst works with Microsoft Security to find, prioritize, and eliminate vulnerabilities end to end. Together they scan and rank risk, prioritize actions by severity and exposure, and flag vulnerable code and databases for modernization. Through GitHub Copilot you can quickly remediate vulnerabilities as applications are modernized, fixing them once and shipping as both modern and hardened. Ready for AI Azure Catalyst works in GitHub Copilot to help teams understand the business logic and dependencies of complex applications and upgrade those apps to run on Azure’s managed services. These upgrades make it easier to connect apps to AI workflows. New previews support modernizing applications and databases together and migrating from BizTalk to Azure Logic Apps. And because Azure Catalyst is built for Azure, it optimizes performance, security, and economics along the way. Microsoft is customer zero for agent-led modernization, putting the same agentic tooling in Azure Catalyst across our estate. Microsoft Quantum and Xbox achieved 80% faster app modernization, while Intune upgraded a key library 75% faster than anticipated. GitHub ported the GitHub Copilot agentic harness—800,000 lines of production code—from TypeScript to Rust. By using these technologies ourselves, we learn firsthand what it takes to modernize complex, production-scale systems, from targeted fixes to large-scale code transformation, and apply those lessons to help you modernize your own environment. For a full breakdown, read the Azure Catalyst announcement blog. To go deeper at Microsoft Ignite, check out these on-demand sessions: BRK412: Rethink modernization end to end with agents BRK409: Modernize faster with AI-powered discovery, planning, and execution BRK410: Accelerating Java, .NET, and database modernization with agents Read more about Azure Catalyst in this blog Run AI across cloud, edge, and devices Across cloud, enterprise infrastructure, edge, physical systems, and personal devices, we’re giving you the power to run AI where your business needs it. Azure Local and flex nodes for AKS extend cloud infrastructure and Kubernetes compute into distributed environments, while extending Microsoft Foundry across these environments. Azure Arc provides consistent infrastructure management and governance end to end. New at Microsoft Ignite, Windows Server 2028 enables AI inference alongside business-critical applications and data, while Windows PCs bring intelligence directly to the devices where people work through local processing. Together, you compose the right infrastructure for each AI workload to best meet data, performance, regulatory, and cost requirements. For a full breakdown, read the Windows Server 2028 blog. To go deeper at Microsoft Ignite, check out these on-demand sessions: BRK418: What’s new and what’s next for Windows Server BRK442: Build sovereign AI with Azure Local and Foundry Local Read more about Windows Server 2028 in this blog Innovate on an open foundation for what comes next The architecture decisions you make today will carry your business for the next decade. Our job is to ensure the systems you depend on now can evolve into an AI-powered future, and that everything you build next runs on an open, co-engineered platform with choice over your models and where your workloads run. The real test of everything we’re introducing is how these solutions perform in your environment. We’ll keep listening and building alongside you. This week, I’m looking forward to Mark Russinovich, Chief Technology Officer (CTO), Deputy Chief Information Security Officer (dCISO), and Technical Fellow, Microsoft Azure and Pavan Davuluri, Executive Vice President, Windows and Devices, discussing why Azure and Windows are the foundation for mission-critical AI, from datacenters to the edge to a billion devices, at INV643: AI infrastructure from cloud to edge. title: [CNCF] Your runtime security tool is not your baseline: Silos dressed as autonomy in cloud native teams
summary: A deadline creates pressure, and a team decides to solve its part of the problem directly. I once saw this play out in a Kubernetes security initiative. The team had capable engineers, a clear objective and a reasonable concern that asking for help might slow them down. They picked a runtime detection tool, deployed it across the clusters and had a dashboard full of events within a week. The missing piece was not the tool. It was the baseline: the shared definition of what normal looks like for those workloads and what should be blocked rather than just reported. Without it, every alert raised the same question: is this expected? The people who could answer that sat in another team, and nobody had asked them early enough. The decision made sense from where the team stood. They had a task, a tool and a plan. What they lacked was the cross-team agreement that makes the tool useful, and confidence that asking for it would get a timely answer. In cloud native engineering, “we can handle this ourselves” sounds like healthy ownership, and often it is. This post is about the cases where it isn’t, and about the artifact that usually exposes the difference: the security baseline. The new version of the silo The old silo was a wall. The new one can be a door that closes without anyone noticing: the team keeps moving and reports progress, but a key conversation never happens. SignalOld siloNew siloLanguage“That is not my job”“We can handle this ourselves”PresenceNobody shows upThe team shows up, does not askFailure modeWork never startsWork starts, then stalls at the missing pieceCostLate, visiblyLate, after looking like progress Autonomy is not automatically a silo. A team that owns its platform and makes its own decisions is what good engineering looks like. The silo appears when autonomy turns into self-sufficiency: the team stops checking who else holds part of the answer and rebuilds knowledge that already exists elsewhere in the organisation. Renaming a team does not fix this either. Platform security, cloud native security and DevSecOps are labels; collaboration still depends on how people work together. Three things make the new silo likely: Deadlines reward visible progress. A deployed DaemonSet and a dashboard are easy to show. Agreeing on expected behaviour, exception handling and verification is less visible, but it decides whether the deployment means anything. Security looks like an approval queue. If every question to a security team turns into a review and a long wait, a well-run engineering team will reasonably try to work around it. That is a design problem for security teams, not a character flaw in platform teams. Prevention is hard to measure. Shipping independently is easy to demonstrate. An early conversation that prevents rework produces a problem that never happens. A tool working as configured is not a control The risk is rarely that a tool fails. It is that a tool works exactly as configured, without a shared understanding of what it is supposed to achieve. The pattern repeats across the cloud native security stack: A runtime detection engine such as Falco ships with general-purpose rules. Turning its output into signal requires knowing what each workload is expected to do, and that knowledge lives with the teams that build and run those workloads. An admission controller such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper can block or only report. Choosing between those modes is a risk decision, not a configuration detail. Kubernetes audit logging produces evidence only if someone has decided what to record, how long to keep it and who reads it. None of these are shortcomings of the projects. They are design dependencies: the tool provides the mechanism, and the organisation has to provide the intent. The baseline is a cross-team artifact A baseline is not a policy document. It is a short, testable set of answers, and every answer maps to something you can configure and verify in a cluster. The question that matters is who has to agree on each one. Baseline questionWhere it lives in the clusterWho has to agreeWhich workloads may run, and with which security context?Pod Security Standards via Pod Security Admission, or equivalent admission policiesPlatform and securityWhich registries and image provenance are accepted?Signature verification with Sigstore enforced at admission (for example Kyverno verifyImages or the Sigstore policy-controller)Security and application teamsWhat is blocked, and what is only reported?Kyverno Enforce or Audit; Gatekeeper deny, warn or dryrun; Pod Security Admission enforce, warn or auditSecurity defines, platform operatesWhat does normal runtime behaviour look like?Falco rules, lists, macros and rule exceptions tuned per workloadApplication teams, with securityWho can approve an exception, and when does it expire?Kyverno PolicyException resources, Gatekeeper constraint exclusions, Falco rule exceptionsA risk owner with authority over the serviceWhich events are retained, for how long, and who reads them?Kubernetes audit policy levels and the log backend’s retentionSecurity operations and platform A note on naming: Pod Security Standards define a profile called baseline. That profile is one useful input, but the baseline in this post is the wider organisational agreement that includes it. Looking at the table, no single team owns every row. A platform team that deploys all of these tools alone has implemented the mechanisms and guessed at the intent. That is the new silo in its most concrete form. Make the baseline cheap to ask about The answer is not to send platform teams back to a security approval queue. It is to make the cross-team parts of the baseline easy to reach. Treating the baseline as code is a practical way to do that, because it uses workflows engineering teams already know: Keep policies in a repository, alongside the admission policies, Falco rules and audit policy that implement them. Make ownership explicit with code owners. A CODEOWNERS file can require review from security for the paths that define block-or-report decisions, and from application teams for the runtime rules that describe their workloads. Ownership stops being implicit knowledge. Turn exceptions into pull requests. Each exception records the policy it bypasses, the workload it applies to, who approved it and when it expires. Expiry needs enforcement too, such as a scheduled CI check that fails when an exception has passed its date. An exception with no expiry is a permanent policy change nobody reviewed. Start in report mode on purpose. Running new policies in Audit or warn first is a good practice, as long as there is an agreed date and owner for the move to enforcement. Otherwise report mode becomes the permanent state. Publish a clear contact and response expectation for each owning team. A code owner who takes three weeks to review is an approval queue with better tooling. Security teams carry half of this. When guidance is hard to find or exceptions are slow, teams have every incentive to work around the process. Autonomy is not the problem. Expensive help is. Four decisions that rarely belong to the same person Once a team acts, four decisions have to be made explicit: DecisionWho should hold itHow it usually failsDefine the expected outcomeSecurity, risk or architectureA policy statement nobody can testImplement and operate itThe team that owns the platform or serviceSecurity ends up doing it, or it is done once and never maintainedAccept the residual riskA role with authority over the service and the budget to remediateWhoever understands the technical detail, or security by defaultVerify it stays effectiveSecurity or another independent functionImplementation is treated as proof, and drift goes unnoticed The third row is where most programmes quietly break. The person who approves an exception must be able to fund its remediation or carry the consequence if it never happens. Someone who can sign but cannot fund is not accepting a risk. They are witnessing it. Frameworks describe the same split. In NIST CSF 2.0, GV.RR-02 asks for roles, responsibilities and authorities to be established, communicated, understood and enforced. GV.RR-03 expects resources to match the risk strategy, and ID.RA-07 asks for exceptions to be assessed, recorded and tracked. In the EU, NIS2 Article 20 and DORA Article 5 place accountability on the management body rather than on a security team. None of these require a team to go it alone. They require that authority, funding and the exception path are explicit. Takeaway A silo is not a team that stopped asking permission. It is a team that stopped asking for help. Deploying a runtime security tool, an admission controller or an audit pipeline is the easy part, and a platform team can do it independently. Defining what those tools should enforce is a cross-team decision, and pretending otherwise is how the new silo forms. A simple habit at kick-off: for each row of the baseline, ask who owns the answer, when it is needed and how to reach them. When work stalls, ask what made going alone seem like the best option before assigning blame. Was guidance easy to find? Could the right people respond in time? Was the exception path clear? Autonomy works best when a team can act, knows where the rest of the answer lives and can reach the people who have it without friction. Trust and collaboration are not the opposite of ownership. They are what make it sustainable. References Kubernetes, Pod Security Standards and Auditing Falco documentation Kyverno documentation OPA Gatekeeper documentation Sigstore documentation NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (CSWP 29): GV.RR-02, GV.RR-03, ID.RA-07 Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS2), Article 20 Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 (DORA), Article 5 This post describes an engineering operating model, not a legal interpretation or a universal assignment of responsibilities. Adapt it to your organization’s structure and risk management process.

title: [Cloudflare] How Cloudflare WAF protects against ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825)
summary: On November 19, 2026, the Ruby team disclosed ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825), a heap buffer overflow in the way Ruby changes the case of strings. Ruby rates the flaw Critical and says it is aware of proofs of concept that achieve remote code execution in some scenarios. Fixes shipped in Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10.The reach is wide. Veria Labs reports that Ruby on Rails and classic-style Sinatra applications reach the bug in their default configuration, before any authentication. Self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, including GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject, Discourse and Chatwoot, shipped an affected Ruby in their latest release at the time of disclosure.Cloudflare WAF blocks ruby2shell for all customers, including those on the Free plan. We have added two rules to both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, with Block as the default action: one for ruby2shell and one for GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, a related integer overflow in Ruby string case conversion fixed in the same releases.The WAF is a compensating control, not a replacement for patching. Exploits can reach the bug through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade Ruby. Our team continues to monitor attack traffic and will update the rules as new techniques appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and get the latest on the vulnerability in the Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.Cloudflare has patched its own systems that use Ruby, and we have found no indication of compromise.What we know about ruby2shellRuby strings carry an encoding, and Ruby still supports many legacy single-byte encodings, such as ISO-8859-1 (Latin-1) and Windows-1252, alongside UTF-8. In a single-byte encoding each character takes one byte, so changing the case of a string usually produces output of the same length.The German sharp s (ß) breaks that assumption. Its uppercase form is two characters, SS. In 14 ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings, Ruby writes those two bytes but checks for room for only one. According to Veria Labs, a string with 21 sharp s characters overflows the output buffer by one byte. The methods that reach the bug are upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?. UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.A one-byte overflow can look harmless. In a memory-corruption exploit, though, a single byte written past the end of a heap buffer can be enough to corrupt an adjacent object or allocator metadata. Ruby says it is aware of proofs of concept that turn this flaw into code execution, and Veria Labs says it will publish its own proof of concept about a week after disclosure. We expect scanning to start soon after.Why default Rails and Sinatra apps are exposedHTML forms can only send GET and POST requests. To simulate PUT, PATCH, or DELETE, many web frameworks accept a _method parameter in a POST request. Rack, the interface most Ruby web frameworks build on, implements this in its MethodOverride middleware, which converts the value of _method to uppercase. Rails includes this middleware by default, and classic-style Sinatra applications enable it. An attacker can send a multipart POST request whose _method part declares a legacy character set and contains a run of sharp s characters. The framework upcases the value while it is still routing the request, before any application code or authentication check runs.Veria Labs reports that other frameworks and plain Rack applications are not exposed by default. Application code that changes the case of strings received in a legacy encoding may still be affected, wherever the string comes from.Who is affectedConditionDetailsRuby versionRuby 3.3.13 and earlier, 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, and 4.0.0 through 4.0.9. Veria Labs reports the bug has been present since Ruby 2.4.0. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached end of life and will not receive the fix.FrameworkRails and classic-style Sinatra in their default configuration. Any other code that changes the case of attacker-controlled strings in a legacy single-byte encoding.Bundled softwareAs of November 19, 2026, Veria Labs lists GitLab 19.6.0, GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5, Mastodon 4.7.5, OpenProject 17.9.7, Discourse 2026.10.1 and Chatwoot 4.20.0 as bundling an affected Ruby in their latest release. Discourse moved its Docker base image to Ruby 4.0.10 on November 19, so rebuilding a Docker install picks up the fix.Distribution packages can backport fixes without changing the Ruby version number, so check the full package version against your distribution's advisory.Six more Ruby flaws in the same releaseRuby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10 also fix six other memory safety flaws, and Ruby says several of them can lead to code execution. One, GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, is an integer overflow in the same string case conversion code, and our second WAF rule covers it. The other five are in Ruby's regular expression engine. Most of them require the application to compile or match a regular expression pattern supplied by the attacker. That is uncommon in web applications, but it does happen in search features, filtering rules and admin tools.How Cloudflare WAF protects youUpgrading every Ruby runtime takes time, especially when Ruby is bundled inside self-hosted products and container images. Cloudflare WAF reduces your exposure while you patch.New managed rules, on for every customerBoth rules are part of the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Ruleset ID efb7b8c949ac4650a09736fc376e9aee), with Block as the default action.Rule descriptionRule IDRulesetDefault actionRuby - Heap Overflow - CVE:CVE-2026-1328257328f23691e44b07892ebd25b19210f1Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset (Free plan)BlockRuby - Heap Overflow - CVE:CVE-2026-1328251afa543a1ed84893b01df04c34402c88Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro, Business and Enterprise plans)BlockRuby - Integer Overflow - GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px8660e37e86444f9f9267ba22e9855f05Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset (Free plan)BlockRuby - Integer Overflow - GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px6defac6a52334542adf4a162daf25922Cloudflare Managed Ruleset (Pro, Business and Enterprise plans)BlockOn the Free plan, the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset runs automatically, so there is nothing to turn on. On paid plans, the rules are active wherever the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed. Because paid plans give you more control over how rulesets are deployed, the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset may not be active on every zone. We recommend checking its status to confirm that it is running. You can use the links in the Zero Wire briefing to go straight to the rules in your dashboard.What the WAF cannot seeA WAF can block an exploit when the malicious input arrives in an HTTP request that passes through Cloudflare. It cannot block every path to the vulnerable code:Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. Requests sent directly to your origin IP address, and traffic between internal services, never reach the WAF. Configure your origin to accept traffic only from Cloudflare, for example with Cloudflare Tunnel or Authenticated Origin Pulls.Other entry points into the same code. Ruby code that changes the case of strings from email, file imports, message queues or background jobs can reach ruby2shell without an HTTP request.Adding defense in depth with WAF attack scoreMemory corruption is usually only the first step. To run commands, an attacker still has to deliver a second-stage payload, such as shell commands or a reverse shell, and then interact with the compromised server. WAF attack score uses machine learning to score each request for remote code execution payloads, which helps catch exploit variations and post-exploitation traffic that signature-based rules can miss. Create a custom rule that blocks or challenges requests with cf.waf.score.rce le 20 on Enterprise plans, or cf.waf.score.class eq "attack" on Business plans.Impact on Cloudflare infrastructureCloudflare has patched its systems that use Ruby against ruby2shell. We have found no indication of compromise and continue to monitor.Patch nowruby2shell turns a one-byte miscalculation in string case conversion into a pre-authentication path to code execution in default Rails and Sinatra apps. With a public proof of concept expected within days, the window to patch is short. Here is what to do:Check your WAF coverage. On the Free plan, the ruby2shell rules are already blocking. On paid plans, confirm the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed and the rules have not been overridden.Upgrade Ruby to 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10 and restart every Ruby process, including background workers. Rebuild container images. Move applications on Ruby 3.2 or earlier to a supported series.Update self-hosted products that bundle Ruby, such as GitLab, GitHub Enterprise Server, Mastodon, OpenProject and Chatwoot, as each vendor releases a fix. Rebuild Discourse Docker installs now.Inventory your runtimes. The Zero Wire briefing includes a prompt you can give an AI agent to find every affected Ruby runtime in your infrastructure.Our WAF analysts will keep updating protections as new techniques appear. Follow the WAF changelog for rule updates.

title: [Cloudflare] How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against phpAfterShell and other critical PHP flaws
summary: On November 19, 2026, the security research company depthfirst disclosed phpAfterShell (CVE-2026-126714), a vulnerability in PHP's default file-based session handler that can lead to remote code execution. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The PHP project fixed it the same day in versions 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, and 8.6.0. These releases fix 16 other security vulnerabilities, six of them also rated critical.Cloudflare’s web application firewall (WAF) blocks known phpAfterShell attack patterns, including for customers on the Free plan. The protection comes from a PHP remote code execution rule we first deployed in October 2026 for the php2shell vulnerabilities. That rule already detected part of the phpAfterShell attack pattern before the vulnerability was disclosed, and on November 19 we updated its detection logic to cover phpAfterShell. The rule is part of both the Cloudflare Free Managed Ruleset and the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset, is enabled by default, and its default action is Block.In the same WAF release, we added three new rules to the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset for paid plans: one for a request smuggling flaw in PHP-FPM (CVE-2026-129289), and two for flaws in PHP's SOAP extension (CVE-2026-15353 and CVE-2026-129506) that PHP fixed in the same releases. These rules are enabled by default with the Log action, because the request patterns they look for can also appear in legitimate traffic, and blocking by default could disrupt it. Customers can review matching requests in Security Events now and change the action to Block once they confirm the rules do not affect legitimate traffic.The WAF is an additional layer of defense, not a replacement for the patch. Several of the critical flaws depend on server configuration or can be reached through paths a WAF does not see, and the only complete fix is to upgrade PHP and restart every worker. Our analysts continue to monitor attack activity and will update the rules as new techniques and variations appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and follow how the vulnerabilities develop in the dedicated Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.There appears to be no indication so far that these vulnerabilities have been exploited. As of November 19, 2026, none of the 17 vulnerabilities was listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and no source we reviewed reports exploitation in the wild.What we know about phpAfterShellPHP stores session data in files by default. When an application calls session_start(), PHP reads the session file and deserializes its content into the $_SESSION array. When the request ends, PHP writes the updated session back to the same file.phpAfterShell is triggered when that write is interrupted. The session file can then hold the beginning of the new session data followed by the end of the old one. On the next request, session_start() deserializes this mixed content. If an attacker controlled the old data, PHP can end up deserializing objects of the attacker's choice.An attacker trying to exploit the flaw is likely to first search for a way to place controlled data in the session. PHP's advisory names two:Session upload progress, a PHP feature that writes information about a running file upload into the session. A remote client can use it to shape the stored data.Applications that store large user-controlled strings in the session.According to PHP, code execution also requires an interruption at a useful point in the write and a suitable deserialization gadget chain in the application. depthfirst reports that it reached code execution without an application gadget by chaining a second, undisclosed memory-corruption bug in a PHP-native class. The sources we reviewed do not establish whether that second bug is fixed in the November 19 releases.depthfirst says it discovered and reported phpAfterShell. The CVE record credits Leo Lin and Asahi as reporters.The other critical flawsThe same releases fix six more critical vulnerabilities. It cannot block every path to these vulnerabilities, including:The deserialization step. phpAfterShell's final step happens inside PHP, when it reads a corrupted session file. The WAF can block the requests that plant the payload, not the read itself.Session data from other sources. If an application copies user-controlled data into the session from a database, a queue or an upstream API, that data may never cross the WAF in a recognizable form.Flaws triggered by server state. CVE-2026-129496, CVE-2026-129481, CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 depend on error logs, diagnostics and worker lifecycle. They do not have dedicated WAF rules, and the patch and the configuration changes below are the way to address them.Traffic that bypasses Cloudflare. This includes internal traffic between services and PHP-FPM listeners exposed directly to a network.Adding defense in depth with WAF attack scoreWAF attack score adds a machine learning layer that scores each request for attack payloads. It is available on Business plans (cf.waf.score.class) and, with a dedicated remote code execution sub-score (cf.waf.score.rce) along with an overall score (cf.waf.score), on Enterprise plans.Attack score complements the managed rules. It will not recognize every serialized object or smuggled FastCGI record on its own, but a working exploit chain usually needs more than one request, and the later stages carry payloads the model is trained to score:Second-stage payloads. Once an attacker can run code, they still need to send commands: shell execution primitives (/bin/sh -c, system(), passthru()), PHP code evaluation (eval(), assert()) or reverse-shell strings in headers, query parameters or request bodies.Webshell traffic. Attackers often drop a small PHP webshell after the initial compromise. Requests that pass operating system commands to that webshell remain visible to attack score.Deploy protections and patchYou can find more information on how to deploy managed rules and attack score in our WAF guide. In short:Check that phpAfterShell protection is active. On the Free plan, no action is needed. On paid plans, make sure the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset is deployed and that the PHP Remote Code Execution Attack #6 rule is set to Block.Review the new rules and switch them to Block. The CVE-2026-129289, CVE-2026-15353 and CVE-2026-129506 rules are in Log mode by default. Review their matches in Security Events, then change their action to Block.Layer attack score. Create a custom rule that blocks or challenges requests with a low remote code execution score, for example cf.waf.score.rce le 20 on Enterprise plans, or cf.waf.score.class eq "attack" on Business plans.Upgrade PHP. Move to 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 or 8.6.0. Rebuild container images and restart the PHP-FPM master or Apache so every worker loads the new binary, then verify the version that serves web requests. After upgrading, check that no php.ini, FPM pool or virtual host still sets session.upload_progress.enabled=1, because an explicit setting overrides the new default.Apply interim mitigations if you cannot upgrade right away. Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and limit the untrusted data you store in sessions. Turn off FastCGI connection reuse. On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0. Fix configuration errors that produce PHP startup warnings, or send PHP errors to syslog instead of a file. Keep PHP-FPM listeners off untrusted networks. These steps reduce exposure; they do not fix the flaws.For a prompt you can give an AI agent to inventory your PHP deployments and check each one against all seven critical CVEs, see the phpAfterShell page on Cloudflare Zero Wire.Update every PHP runtime nowphpAfterShell turns an interrupted file write in PHP's default session handler into a path to code execution, and it arrived in the same release as six other critical flaws. With technical details now public, we expect exploit attempts to follow. Cloudflare WAF blocks known phpAfterShell attack patterns for every customer, including the Free plan, and paid plans have new rules for the PHP-FPM and SOAP flaws. The fix is still to upgrade PHP and restart the services that use it.

title: [Microsoft Azure] Microsoft Ignite 2026: What’s new in Azure, the platform purpose-built for AI
summary: Azure at Microsoft Ignite 2026: The headlines Azure AI core: AI on infrastructure you control. Azure Cobalt 200: Our highest-performing general-purpose virtual machines (VMs). Azure Catalyst: Agent-led modernization from plan to code. Agentic cloud operations: Agents that keep your cloud running well. Azure HorizonDB and Fabric HorizonDB: PostgreSQL for AI apps and analytics. Fabric apps: Governed apps built on trusted data. Microsoft IQ: Context for every agent. Over the past year, my conversations with customers have changed. A year ago, the question was which model to choose. Now it’s how to put agents to work on the processes that run the business, and how to trust them to do it. With the same frontier models available to everyone, the advantage comes from what no one else has: your context. It’s how your business runs, what your people know, and the systems and data you’ve spent years building. That’s your IQ. It’s your intellectual property, so it should stay yours, and it should work wherever your people and agents do. Our job is to make every layer beneath your agents better, from the infrastructure that runs them and the estate they act on to the apps they power and the business context that tells them how your company works. Azure is the foundation of Frontier Transformation. We engineer Azure as one system, so the knowledge an agent needs stays governed and the security you use to protect your people extends to the agents acting for them. And because we’re evolving the open, cloud-native platform you already rely on, you don’t have to start over. See what Azure can do for your business As Satya Nadella shared at Microsoft Build in June, we added more datacenter capacity in 18 months than in Azure’s first decade. Combined with more regions than any other cloud provider, you can scale your AI workloads globally with confidence as demand grows. This week at Microsoft Ignite, we’re sharing what’s new across every layer of the platform. New capabilities spanning compute, storage, and networking let you run AI at scale with the control of your own infrastructure, without having to build, secure, and operate all of it yourself. Azure Catalyst brings agent-led modernization together in one experience from estate to code. PostgreSQL now has two homes at Microsoft: Azure HorizonDB, generally available for mission-critical scale, and the new Fabric HorizonDB, which connects your PostgreSQL apps to analytics and AI. And Fabric apps, now generally available, let your teams turn trusted enterprise data into working apps. We’re also introducing Microsoft IQ, the enterprise context management platform that helps you build your own IQ and put it to work in every app and agent. It also gives your teams a path on Azure to build, run, and continuously improve those agents. Run AI at scale with the control you choose It starts with the infrastructure that runs your agents. As they take on real work, you should be able to run them on your terms, with your choice of models, your data, and where they run. That control lets you find the right balance of performance and cost for each workload and adapt as models and needs change. But control comes with real work and risk. Platform teams end up assembling and operating much of the AI stack themselves and stretching GPUs to keep up with shifting demand. Agents that reach models, tools, and data and run code on their own open new security gaps, putting sensitive data at risk. Teams want the control of running their own AI infrastructure without taking on all the manual toil of building, securing, and operating it. Building the AI core on Azure That’s what we’re bringing to Azure. New capabilities across compute, storage, and networking come together as one AI foundation, so you keep control of your models and workloads while Azure takes on the work underneath. Build AI with Microsoft Foundry in a fully managed experience and run it at scale with Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) when you need more control over performance, security, and cost. Ignite session: AI infrastructure from cloud to Edge Watch now ↗ Azure sets up and tunes the infrastructure for you, so your teams spend less time on configuration and more time moving models and agents into production. Workloads are placed based on available capacity, so your GPU investment goes further as demand grows. Security is enforced centrally across agents, models, and tools, giving security teams consistent controls wherever agents run. And because it’s built on open-source projects, your workloads stay portable, including to your own servers outside Azure, keeping your options open as your needs change. The result is AI that scales with your business, on infrastructure you control. To hear how organizations are operating AI at scale, watch Mark Russinovich and Pavan Davuluri in the innovation session “AI Infrastructure from cloud to edge.” Strengthening every layer of your AI estate with Azure Cobalt 200 Agents reason, make decisions, and run continuously, and that’s reshaping what cloud infrastructure needs to deliver. That’s why we design Azure as one system, from silicon to servers to services. We pair our own Maia and Cobalt chips with the latest from NVIDIA and AMD, so every workload runs on the right silicon for the job. Our strategy focuses on building performance, efficiency, and security into every layer. The result is AI that’s faster and more economical to run at scale, on a roadmap you can plan around. Ignite session: cobalt 200… Watch now ↗ Azure Cobalt 200 virtual machines, our highest-performing general-purpose VMs, are now generally available. Designed from the ground up for scale-out, cloud native, and agentic AI workloads, these VMs deliver up to 50% better CPU performance compared to our Cobalt 100 VMs. Together with Maia, they give you an infrastructure you can plan around. Read about the latest Azure Cobalt updates in this blog Agent-led modernization and operations, from estate to code Agents are only as useful as the systems they can act on. Much of what makes your company unique is built into your applications and databases and years of business logic your teams rely on. Modernizing puts existing apps and data to work in new AI-powered experiences, helps teams ship faster, and lowers the cost and risk of running older systems, creating a more adaptable foundation for growth. Getting there isn’t easy. Modernizing can mean mapping complex systems and changing code that few people fully understand. Keeping the estate running well means sorting through constant signals with little knowledge on what matters most. And as agents take on more of that work, teams need to let them act while keeping the oversight your business requires. That’s why we’re bringing agents to both, from estate to code. Azure Catalyst helps you modernize applications, code, and databases from plan to execution. And new capabilities in Azure Copilot, Azure SRE Agent, and Azure Monitor help keep your cloud and databases running well, with people in control. Modernize for AI with Azure Catalyst Azure Catalyst is a new unified experience for agentic modernization. It brings discovery, planning, migration, modernization, and code intelligence together, so IT teams and developers work from the same plan across infrastructure, applications, and data. Azure Catalyst modernizes the technology you already have into a foundation for AI, putting the business logic in your existing applications to work in new AI-powered experiences and agentic business processes. Ignite session: rethink modernization… Watch now ↗ For IT teams, Azure Catalyst agent extends from migration planning into deeper modernization and execution. For developers, GitHub Copilot modernization carries that plan into code in the tools they already use, with agent governance rulebooks and bring-your-own-model support that customizes your modernization project to the specifications of each business. And Azure Catalyst delivers a deeper understanding of how enterprise applications work, so teams can assess the impact of changes, modernize faster, and find where legacy processes could be reimagined with AI. Ignite session: modernize faster with ai… Watch now ↗ Modernization can also close security gaps. End-of-support runtimes, unpatched dependencies, and aging code widen your threat surface. Azure Catalyst works with Microsoft Security to fix that: Microsoft Perception and MDASH rank vulnerabilities across your estate and code, Azure Catalyst identifies vulnerable code and databases to modernize first, and GitHub Copilot turns those findings into fixes in the same pass. Each app comes out more secure than it went in. Learn more about Azure AI foundation and Azure Catalyst in this blog Keep your cloud running well with agentic operations As applications scale across hybrid infrastructure, microservices, and AI workloads, leading organizations are moving to operating models where insight flows directly into action. That’s the idea behind agentic operations: AI agents, guided by your intent, continuously observe, reason, and help take action across the cloud lifecycle. Signals feed coordinated workflows that improve performance, cost, and reliability as systems run, with people kept in control. At Microsoft Ignite, we’re bringing that model to more of your estate. Azure Copilot‘s deployment agent, now generally available, helps you go from requirements described in natural language to deployed cloud workloads. You can even extend agentic operations to Oracle and SAP with Azure Workload Center, now in limited preview. Ignite session: put ai agents to work… Watch now ↗ Azure SRE Agent brings agentic operations into secure production environments, with new enterprise controls in preview, while Microsoft Entra Agent ID and Agent 365 give central teams a consistent way to discover, govern, and audit agents throughout their lifecycle. We’re also giving agents richer data and understanding so they can detect issues earlier, diagnose problems faster, and take more effective action. Azure Monitor health models, now generally available, give agents a real-time view of your application architecture and business priorities, so they can recommend fixes. Learn more about agentic operations in this blog Build the next generation of AI apps Then there are the apps your agents power, where business data becomes business value. The question for every organization is how quickly it can move from idea to an app the entire business can rely on. Today, the people building AI apps span the whole organization. Developers are creating mission-critical systems and new apps with agents, while teams across the business are describing the app they need in Copilot. Each needs something different from the platform, but every app needs to connect to business data and run under governance IT can trust. We’re building one foundation for all of them, and it starts with PostgreSQL, the database of choice for a growing share of developers. With Azure HorizonDB and Fabric HorizonDB, you can run PostgreSQL wherever your apps need it, from mission-critical systems to analytics and AI. Fabric apps builds on that foundation, so teams can turn business data into working apps, whether they start in code or in conversation. Power your AI apps with PostgreSQL on Azure HorizonDB and Fabric HorizonDB The apps developers build now reason over data, call models, and act for users, so the database underneath has to bring transactions, vectors, and AI together at mission-critical scale. Azure HorizonDB, now generally available, is a fully managed, PostgreSQL-compatible database built for that work. It delivers millisecond latency with built-in vector indexing, so your apps can find, reason over, and act on data in one place. Enterprise-grade security comes built in, and developers can work in tools they already know, including GitHub Copilot and Visual Studio Code. ignite session: data foundations for modern apps… Watch now ↗ We’re also extending the power of PostgreSQL directly into Microsoft Fabric. Fabric HorizonDB, now in public preview, brings a serverless, Fabric-native PostgreSQL experience alongside SQL database in Fabric and Cosmos DB in Fabric. By bringing operational databases, analytics, and AI together on a unified, governed platform, developers can build intelligent applications with less data movement and complexity. Fabric HorizonDB will also serve as the PostgreSQL backend for Fabric apps. To simplify database management across environments, Database Hub in Fabric is now generally available. It provides a unified experience to discover, monitor, and manage databases across Azure, on-premises environments, and Fabric, with Fabric Copilot highlighting what needs attention. Read the latest Microsoft Databases announcements in this blog Turn ideas into governed enterprise-ready apps with Fabric apps, now generally available Great ideas for apps come from every corner of the business, and with Copilot, people can build one in minutes. But taking it from prototype to production on trusted data remains the biggest hurdle. Fabric apps, now generally available, bring together the backend services applications need with direct access to trusted data in Fabric, built-in security, and enterprise governance. Developers and coding agents build in code with open-source tools, and Fabric provisions everything from databases to authentication, with no infrastructure to manage. This makes it easier to turn ideas into enterprise-ready applications that can scale across the organization. ignite session: build like a startup… Watch now ↗ We’re also extending Fabric’s role as the data foundation for AI-powered applications. With the new Microsoft Copilot integration, now in Frontier public preview, anyone can describe the app they need and bring it to life, with the option to use Fabric as a ready-to-use data backend providing databases, storage, and data APIs. We’re also introducing Copilot Credits as a new usage-based billing option for Microsoft Fabric, providing greater flexibility alongside existing capacity-based options. Power BI creators can now build more than static reports. With a new agentic app creation experience in Power BI Desktop, now in preview, they can turn their existing semantic models into interactive apps that capture input, update data, and support operational workflows. Learn more about Fabric apps in the Ignite Microsoft Fabric blog Ground every agent in your business context with Microsoft IQ Most organizations already have the knowledge their agents need. It lives in the semantic models your analysts built in Power BI, the documents and procedures your teams rely on, the conversations happening across Microsoft 365, and the systems of record you run every day, like SAP and Oracle. The problem is that it’s scattered, so every new agent starts from zero and every team rebuilds the same context. That’s why we’re introducing Microsoft IQ, the enterprise context management platform for building your organization’s IQ. It brings together Work IQ, Fabric IQ, Foundry IQ, Web IQ, and more than 350 connectors, so the knowledge your agents need is captured once, governed in one place, and reused by every agent and app. At the heart of Microsoft IQ are new business plugins, now available as part of the Frontier program. Business plugins turn what your teams know into trusted context, skills, and tools that anyone across the business can reuse. Take a supply chain disruption. The foundation underneath Microsoft IQ brings Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Fabric together in one path, built on Azure, to build, run, and continuously improve agents. And Agent 365 gives IT one place to observe, govern, and secure them. ignite session: Harnessing Your IQ… Watch now ↗ Your IQ stays yours, and it isn’t locked into one assistant. See how the Australian Energy Market Operator uses Microsoft IQ to help keep Australia’s power grid secure: Nearly 60,000 customers already use Microsoft IQ today. And because every agent builds on the same context, each one you add makes the next one better. Learn more about Microsoft IQ in this blog Experience these innovations at Microsoft Ignite Every agent you build is only as good as what it knows about your business. That’s why we’re making sure your IQ, the context that makes your company unique, is available to your agents across every layer of Azure, with governance and security built in. title: [Docker] The Trust Layer: Securing Agentic AI with Docker AI Governance
summary: The Agent Trust Gap The security problem changes once an AI agent can do more than answer a prompt. It can execute code, access files, connect to services, and call external tools. That creates a new security question for enterprises: how do you give an agent enough freedom to be useful without giving it more access than it actually needs? A model decision is not automatically an authorized action. That distinction becomes important the moment an agent can turn a model output into an action in a real system. The answer can’t rely only on the model. Agent behavior can vary, while security controls need to be clear and enforceable. That means putting controls around the environment where the agent runs, what it can access, which tools it can use, and what happens when a policy allows or blocks an action. For a CISO, this creates a trust gap. Approving the use of AI agents means being able to answer more than whether the model is capable: what access does the agent have, where are those boundaries enforced, and what evidence is available afterward? The goal is to let teams adopt agents without making model behavior itself the security boundary. Docker AI Governance approaches this through three areas: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility. Together, they address three practical questions security teams need answered: Where can the agent operate? What can it do? And can we see what happened? In this article, I use “trust layer” as shorthand for the infrastructure between what an agent wants to do and what the organization actually allows it to do. There is a related trust question too: what software artifacts are these agentic workflows building and using? Docker Hardened Images address that software supply-chain side of the problem, alongside the runtime controls discussed below. Figure 1: The three layers of Docker AI Governance: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility. Sandbox Policies: Where Can the Agent Operate? An agent needs enough access to get real work done. A coding agent may need to install packages, build containers, edit project files, or connect to external services. The security challenge is deciding where those actions are allowed before the agent starts taking them. Docker Sandboxes give each agent an isolated microVM environment a lightweight virtual machine with its own Docker Engine, filesystem, and network. Docker AI Governance adds policy around that environment so security teams can control network and filesystem access centrally. Network policies can allow or block specific domains, IP ranges, and ports. Filesystem policies control which host paths can be mounted into a sandbox and whether that access is read-only or read-write. These controls are enforced at the network proxy and filesystem mount layers rather than depending on the agent to follow an instruction. For an organization, that means the same boundaries can follow developers across their sandboxes instead of being configured differently on every machine. Teams still get the access they need for their work, but an individual agent cannot simply expand those boundaries on its own. A developer can check the effective boundary before starting the agent: $ sbx policy check network api.anthropic.com Allowed: api.anthropic.com $ sbx policy check network blocked.example.com Denied: blocked.example.com The important part is that the result comes from the active policy, not from an instruction the agent is expected to follow. This answers the first governance question: Where can the agent operate? MCP Tool Governance: What Can the Agent Do? Once an agent has a controlled place to run, the next question is what it should be allowed to do through external tools. MCP (Model Context Protocol) gives agents a common way to connect to external tools, services, and capabilities, but that also expands what an agent can act on. For enterprise use, making a tool available should not automatically mean every agent can use it. Docker AI Governance puts policy around MCP activity handled through Docker’s MCP Gateway. Administrators can control which MCP servers may be registered and what agents can do through them, including tool calls, resources, prompts, and approval requirements. These organization policies are written in Cedar, a policy language used to express authorization rules. When MCP policy enforcement is active, governed requests are denied unless a matching policy permits them. For example, a policy can permit read-only tool calls for a specific registered MCP server: permit (principal, action == MCP::Action::"invokeTool", resource) when { resource in MCP::Server::"example" && resource.readOnly == true }; Here, readOnly comes from the MCP tool’s annotations. Those annotations are supplied by the server and are advisory, so this example relies on metadata provided by that server. This makes tool access an explicit policy decision rather than something left to each agent or developer to configure independently. A team can be given access to the tools it needs, while other servers or actions remain unavailable. Policies can also require confirmation for specific tool calls when an action needs an additional checkpoint. One boundary is worth making clear: MCP policies apply to activity handled by Docker’s MCP Gateway. If an agent connects directly to a remote MCP server from inside a sandbox, that connection falls under the sandbox’s network policy instead. With the environment constrained and tool access governed, we can answer the second question: What can the agent do? Audit + Visibility: Can We See What Happened? Setting a policy is only part of the job. Security teams also need to know when that policy was applied, what action triggered it, and whether the action was allowed or denied. Docker AI Governance records sandbox policy decisions and sandbox session events as structured audit records. Each record captures details such as the principal, action, target, decision, and time. The records contain governance metadata rather than the contents of prompts or agent responses. Audit records can be kept locally or delivered to the cloud. With cloud delivery enabled, teams can search the organization-wide record, export it for further analysis, or forward events into existing SIEM (security information and event management) workflows. Denied actions are especially useful. A team can see not only that an action failed, but that a governance rule blocked it and why. Allowed decisions matter too: they provide a record of how policy was applied while the agent was working. Current audit coverage includes Docker Sandboxes policy decisions and sandbox session events. The same schema can support additional Docker AI sources as they become available. That closes the third part of the governance loop: Can we see what happened? A Trusted Software Supply Chain: Docker Hardened Images AI Governance controls access around the agent at runtime. There is a separate question that matters to the workflows those agents participate in: what container images and software artifacts are they building, testing, or deploying? Docker Hardened Images provide minimal, secure, and production-ready container images, Helm charts, and system packages maintained by Docker. In practical terms, this gives teams evidence about what is inside an image and how that image was produced. Docker Hardened Images include signed SBOMs, VEX information, cryptographic signatures, and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance. Instead of simply trusting where an image came from, teams can inspect what is inside it and verify information about how it was built. For organizations with additional compliance requirements, Docker also provides FIPS-enabled and STIG-ready variants through relevant DHI offerings. These capabilities sit alongside the broader DHI security and supply-chain controls rather than making any single standard the foundation by itself. AI Governance and Docker Hardened Images solve different parts of the trust problem. Governance controls the authority an agent has while it works; DHI helps establish trust in the container artifacts that the workflow depends on. Figure 2: Docker Hardened Images combine minimal container images with signed supply-chain metadata and verifiable build provenance. Putting the Three Layers Together Consider a developer using a coding agent to investigate an issue, update a service, and use an approved internal tool along the way. The agent begins inside a Docker Sandbox. It can work with the project and run the commands needed for the task, but its access is still bounded by policy. If it tries to reach a network destination or mount a host path that the organization has not allowed, the applicable sandbox policy can block that access. Now suppose the agent needs an MCP tool to look up information from another service. The request goes through Docker’s MCP Gateway, where organization policy determines whether that server and tool are permitted. A routine lookup might be allowed, while a more sensitive tool call could require confirmation or remain unavailable altogether. For governance activity currently covered by AI Governance Audit Logs, Docker records the policy decision and relevant session metadata. Security teams can see who initiated the activity, what policy-controlled action was evaluated, and whether it was allowed or denied. Those records can then feed the organization’s existing monitoring and SIEM workflow. If that same agent builds or tests a containerized application, the software entering the workflow matters too. Docker Hardened Images provide a more verifiable software foundation for that workflow, while AI Governance controls what the agent is authorized to do at runtime. The model is still making decisions about how to complete the task. What changes is the authority around those decisions. The agent can work autonomously inside the boundaries the organization has defined, while access outside those boundaries remains a policy decision. That is the practical value of the three layers working together: Sandbox Policies define where the agent can operate. MCP Tool Governance defines what tools it can use. Audit + Visibility shows how governed activity was handled. Taken together, the pattern is straightforward: define the boundary, check it before the agent starts working, enforce it while the agent is running, and use the resulting audit trail to understand what happened. If a boundary needs to change, the policy changes, not the expectation that the model will simply behave differently. Autonomy Without Unbounded Authority The challenge with agentic AI is not simply that agents can make decisions. It is that those decisions can now lead directly to actions. That makes the boundary around the agent just as important as the model itself. Docker AI Governance addresses that boundary through Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility: controlling where agents can operate, what tools they can use, and how governed activity is recorded. Docker Hardened Images address a related supply-chain concern by helping teams work with smaller, verifiable container artifacts. The goal is not to remove autonomy from agents. It is to make sure autonomy does not automatically come with unlimited authority. As agents take on more real work, that distinction will matter more and more.
