title: [Amazon AWS] Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator
summary: Today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), the AWS SDKs, and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub. You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker. How it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/. You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged. From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region. The emulator is implemented in Rust so that it stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop. It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS. If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally. Let’s try it out To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023. The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/, so it’s on the path. PKG=https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest sudo dnf install -y $PKG/aws-emulator-x86_64.rpm aws-emulator -v On macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image. I started the emulator with aws-emulator. It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297, so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file. aws-emulator In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials. export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=https://127.0.0.1:9297 export AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/emulator_credentials export AWS_CONFIG_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/config export AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true export AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION=true export AWS_REGION=us-east-1 export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1 unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN AWS_PROFILE The emulator generates new keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR, so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000. curl --cacert ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem https://127.0.0.1:9297/__admin/health aws sts get-caller-identity Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it. $ aws s3 mb s3://local-getting-started make_bucket: local-getting-started $ echo "hello from the emulator" > hello.txt $ aws s3 cp hello.txt s3://local-getting-started/ upload: ./hello.txt to s3://local-getting-started/hello.txt $ aws s3 ls s3://local-getting-started/ With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them. Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account. kiro> Using the local AWS Emulator (the environment variables are already set in this shell), create a DynamoDB table "kiro-demo" with a string key "id", put an item {id: "item-1", msg: "hello from kiro"}, then read it back with get-item. $ aws dynamodb create-table --table-name kiro-demo \ --attribute-definitions AttributeName=id,AttributeType=S \ --key-schema AttributeName=id,KeyType=HASH \ --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST $ aws dynamodb put-item --table-name kiro-demo \ --item '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}, "msg": {"S": "hello from kiro"}}' $ aws dynamodb get-item --table-name kiro-demo --key '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}}' To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual. Using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java. For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust. You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the  section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process. use aws_emulator_embedded::{AwsEmulatorEmbedded, EmbeddedOptions}; use aws_sdk_dynamodb::types::{ AttributeDefinition, AttributeValue, BillingMode, KeySchemaElement, KeyType, ScalarAttributeType, }; # async fn put_then_get_returns_the_item() { let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded::new(EmbeddedOptions::default()); let config = aws_config::defaults(aws_config::BehaviorVersion::latest()) .http_client(emulator.http_client()) .region(aws_config::Region::new("us-east-1")) .credentials_provider(emulator.aws_credentials_provider()) .load() .await; let ddb = aws_sdk_dynamodb::Client::new(&config); ddb.create_table() .table_name("emulator-demo-table") .attribute_definitions( AttributeDefinition::builder() .attribute_name("id").attribute_type(ScalarAttributeType::S) .build().unwrap()) .key_schema( KeySchemaElement::builder() .attribute_name("id").key_type(KeyType::Hash) .build().unwrap()) .billing_mode(BillingMode::PayPerRequest) .send().await.unwrap(); ddb.put_item() .table_name("emulator-demo-table") .item("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into())) .item("msg", AttributeValue::S("hi".into())) .send().await.unwrap(); let got = ddb.get_item() .table_name("emulator-demo-table") .key("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into())) .send().await.unwrap(); assert_eq!(got.item().unwrap().get("msg").unwrap().as_s().unwrap(), "hi"); } When it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off. How we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates. With each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better. If the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an issue in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub. How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeCommit, so it stays current with AWS as those models change. One group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an issue for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository. How we keep it secure Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships. Security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production. Now available AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation. If you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. To get started, visit the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub and see the AWS Emulator documentation. Updated on November 12, 2026: Added links to the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

title: [CNCF] How to support your app on Kubernetes environments you don’t control
summary: Running an application in Kubernetes is one thing, but supporting that application in Kubernetes environments your customers run is something else entirely. You don’t control the cluster configuration, its upgrade schedule, the surrounding tooling, or the process for investigating an incident. But customers will still look to you when your application won’t install, an upgrade breaks, or a workload behaves differently in their environment than they expected. That doesn’t mean customer-managed Kubernetes deployments can’t work, but it does mean support has to account for the variation you’ll see in real clusters. No Two Customer Environments Are Alike You’ll definitely have two customers (or more!) who both say they run Kubernetes and yet have very different environments. One may run a managed Kubernetes service in a public cloud. Another may operate its own infrastructure. They may use different Kubernetes versions, networking configurations, ingress controllers, storage classes, image registries, security policies, observability tools, or access controls. Those differences affect how your application deploys and how your team supports it. A chart that installs cleanly in your reference architecture may fail because a customer’s admission policies reject a required permission, their storage configuration doesn’t meet your application’s requirements, or their cluster runs a Kubernetes version you haven’t tested yet or no longer support. Unfortunately, your customer still experiences that as a problem with your application. That’s why your team needs a documented view of what the application requires from the cluster, and what falls outside the support boundary. At a minimum, customers need to know: Which Kubernetes versions and distributions you support Which permissions, policies, and cluster capabilities the application needs What networking, ingress, DNS, certificate, secret management, and storage configuration the application expects What resources the application needs to run reliably Which logs, events, metrics, and configuration details your support team will need during an escalation. With bonus points for providing commands directly. The goal isn’t to make every customer environment identical (you can’t). Instead, you need to define a supported operating model so every deployment doesn’t turn into a new discovery process for your customer support team. Customers Won’t Upgrade on Your Schedule Your application roadmap may assume customers will move to newer Kubernetes versions quickly. A quick reality check: most won’t. Customers have their own release schedules, validation processes, maintenance windows, compliance requirements, internal dependencies, and risk thresholds. Even when they want to upgrade, their platform team may have a long list of cluster add-ons, integrations, and workloads to validate first. Like any other software, Kubernetes and different components in its ecosystem change over time. APIs are deprecated and removed, version compatibility varies across control-plane and node components, and the upstream project supports release branches for only the three most recent minor releases. Your team needs a compatibility policy that answers a few basic questions: Which Kubernetes versions do you support today? Which versions are approaching the end of support? How much notice do customers get before you stop supporting a version? What does a customer need to do if an application release depends on a newer Kubernetes capability? Can you offer a documented workaround when a customer can’t upgrade immediately? If the answer to every compatibility problem is to update Kubernetes, customers will quickly find that your support isn’t aligned with how they operate. Your team needs to explain what’s incompatible, why it matters, and the easiest path to return to a supported configuration. Kubernetes Expertise Has to Be Customer-Facing A general application support team can’t diagnose every Kubernetes issue. When a product runs inside a cluster your customer manages, customer-facing teams need enough Kubernetes depth to identify where the problem really lives. That doesn’t mean every support employee has to operate production clusters. It does mean someone working directly with customers needs to understand the difference between an application issue, a deployment-configuration issue, and a cluster-level issue. For example, a pod stuck in Pending may point to unavailable capacity, resource requests that don’t fit on available nodes, a scheduling constraint, or a policy that prevents placement. An image pull failure may involve registry access, credentials, network connectivity, or image policy enforcement. Those details determine who needs to take the next action and what evidence they need to act on it. Your customer-facing team needs dedicated Kubernetes expertise that can: Ask for the right diagnostic information early Review Kubernetes events, pod status, and relevant logs Identify when a customer platform, security, networking, or infrastructure team needs to get involved Explain the issue in terms each stakeholder can act on Escalate to engineering with enough environmental context to investigate effectively Getting accurate answers to these questions matters because the person opening a support case may not own the cluster. The application team probably owns the deployment. A platform team probably owns Kubernetes. Security owns policies. Another infrastructure team may own networking, storage, or identity. Someone on your team needs to help move the issue between those groups. Build for Variation You can’t control every Kubernetes environment where customers run your application. You can control whether your support model treats that variation as expected or as a surprise. So make sure you have a plan for it by: Defining what you support. Documenting the requirements that matter. Testing the Kubernetes versions and deployment conditions you commit to supporting. Setting a clear upgrade and deprecation policy. Making Kubernetes expertise available during onboarding, deployment, escalation, and ongoing support. The support model changes when a provider manages the Kubernetes layer alongside the customer. Instead of troubleshooting an application across an unknown mix of cluster configurations, versions, networking, and add-ons, the provider and customer can work from a more clearly defined operating foundation. title: [CNCF] Optimizing Kubernetes admission control: Where Kyverno’s CEL admission cost actually goes
summary: Kyverno’s CEL (Common Expression Language)-based engines exist to evaluate policy expressions. So when we profiled the admission path, we expected to find the bulk of the cost in CEL evaluation. It was not there. About 86% of what the engine allocated went into preparing the object for evaluation, and almost none of it into evaluating policy. We went looking because a public benchmark put Kyverno behind the alternatives. Those benchmarks measured the legacy ClusterPolicy JMESPath engine, which did have a real regression at the time, and the usual answer was to point people at the newer CEL-based engine instead. That answer was right but incomplete: we had not checked what the CEL engine itself was spending its time on. This post is about where that performance cost came from, why it grew with the number of policies you deploy, and what removing it did. The fix ships in Kyverno 1.19.2. Please read the limitations section before you quote any number here. And as always, run your own tests in your environments, for real-world accuracy. What the profile showed Kyverno’s CEL engines evaluate policies against a CEL activation: a set of variables your policy expressions can reference. One of those variables is request, the AdmissionRequest the API server sent, converted into the unstructured map form CEL understands. Here is a heap profile of the ValidatingPolicy engine handling admission requests, before and after the change, by share of total allocated bytes: Before, ConvertObjectToUnstructured accounted for 86.8% of everything the engine allocated. CEL evaluation itself barely registered. After, object conversion falls to 2.9%, and the largest single frame becomes evaluateWithData — the code that actually runs your policy expressions. The same pattern shows up in the MutatingPolicy engine, which was paying a smaller but still substantial version of the same cost: One caveat on reading those profiles: the post-fix benchmark completes more iterations in the same time because it is faster, so the two profiles have different absolute totals. Compare the shares, not the raw bytes. Per-request figures come from the benchmark table further down. Why: the same object, converted once per policy The API server sends the admitted object as raw JSON bytes. CEL cannot read bytes, so Kyverno parses them into the map form CEL understands before it can evaluate anything against them. That conversion happened inside the loop over matched policies rather than before it. With the Pod Security Standards set, roughly 16 policies match a typical Pod creation — so Kyverno parsed the same Pod 16 times, same input, same output, every time. The cost grew with your policy count and with the size of the object being admitted: O(policies), where it should have been O(1). The object does not change between policies. There was never a reason to convert it more than once. The fix: convert once per request The change moves the conversion out of the per-policy loop. Kyverno builds the CEL request value once, before the loop starts, and every matched policy reuses it. Doing that without changing what policies see takes some care. The expensive part of the conversion is the admitted object itself, so Kyverno converts a copy of the request with that object temporarily blanked out — which leaves only cheap fields to walk — and splices the object back in afterwards. The same conversion code still produces the result, so the output matches what policies saw before rather than being a reimplementation that someone has to keep in sync by hand. Keeping policy behavior identical The first attempt used a single shared builder for every CEL engine. Testing caught that this quietly changed how policies behave, because the engines had never agreed on what request.object meant in the first place. Validating and generating policies saw the object exactly as the API server sent it. Mutating policies saw a normalized version. The two also disagreed about what an empty object looks like to CEL, which matters for operations like DELETE where one side is absent. Unifying them would have changed the result of expressions people already have deployed. That is a conversation worth having, but not one a performance fix should start on its own. So each engine keeps the contract it already had, sharing one fast implementation underneath. Equivalence tests pin this down: they run the original code as the reference and compare its output against the new one field by field, across every request type, so any drift fails the build. What changed The benchmark calls the engine directly with a roughly 50 KB Pod and a varying number of matched policies. It times the engine alone — building the request value, matching, and evaluating CEL. It does not include the webhook round trip, the API server, or etcd, so these are not end-to-end admission latencies. Matched policiesAllocations beforeAllocations afterEngine time beforeEngine time after12,3278540.31 ms0.10 ms1637,0552,7184.91 ms0.16 ms64148,1318,67220.01 ms0.36 ms The MutatingPolicy engine improves on the same curve, from 258,943 to 52,689 allocations and 10.59 ms to 2.97 ms at 64 policies. The slope is the point, not the headline multiple. Before the change, allocations grew about 63 times going from 1 policy to 64. After, about 10 times — and that residual growth is CEL evaluation, which is the work you deployed the policies to get. Object preparation is now constant per request instead of proportional to how many policies you run. Practically: adding policies to a Kyverno deployment used to carry a hidden per-policy serialization cost on top of the evaluation you asked for. It no longer does. Image verification too The image verification engine had the same pattern, with its own private copy of the conversion code, so it got the same fix. The gain there is memory rather than speed: image verification spends most of its time fetching signatures and attestations over the network, and that part does not change. How this compares to native admission policies With the per-policy tax gone, it is worth asking where Kyverno’s CEL engine actually sits against the API server’s own ValidatingAdmissionPolicy. Running the same 16 Pod Security Standards policies through both engines on one cluster, the answer depends on how many policies you enforce: At one policy, native is ahead: about 9.2 ms against Kyverno’s 12.8 ms. At the full 16-policy set, Kyverno is ahead: about 20 ms against native’s 29 ms. Those numbers were measured on Kyverno 1.19.0, which predates the change described above. The Kyverno side of that chart should now be better than shown; we have not re-run the comparison. The two engines pay their costs differently. Native dispatches each policy separately on the API server, so its cost grows with the number of policies you enforce. Kyverno pays once per request to receive the object over a webhook, and that cost is shared across however many policies then evaluate. With only a policy or two, native is ahead. Once you are running a realistic set, Kyverno matches it and can come out ahead. That framing only became accurate with this fix. Kyverno’s cost was not fixed per request before it — it was per policy, which is exactly why the curve looked the way it did. The CPU side is more one-sided. Under matched load, Kyverno’s engine used about 3.2 cores against the API server’s 8.2 for native. The surprise in the API server profile is that 67% of its CPU sits in the policy dispatch machinery while the actual CEL bytecode execution is about 5.5% — the cost is dispatching 16 policies and building an input for each, not evaluating them. And that load lands on the control plane, which you cannot scale horizontally the way you can scale a Kyverno deployment. Both numbers come from a single-host setup where the webhook hop is loopback and effectively free. On a real multi-node cluster that hop costs real latency on every Kyverno request, which narrows the latency gap and matters most at low policy counts. The CPU finding does not depend on topology. The legacy engine, briefly The benchmarks that prompted this work measured ClusterPolicy, the older non-CEL engine, so it is worth saying what happened there. We reproduced the regression across four releases, each on a fresh cluster, run in shuffled order over eight rounds so no version was systematically favored, and compared everything against 1.13.6. The regression is real — between 12% and 23% depending on load — and it appears between 1.16.4 and 1.17.0. That is where the engine started copying its entire evaluation context on every checkpoint, in order to fix a separate bug where one rule’s data could leak into the next. The fix keeps that guarantee but stops paying for it upfront: it takes a shallow snapshot and only copies a value when something actually writes to it. The benchmark returns to roughly its pre-regression level, and the rule isolation still holds, pinned by a test that fails on the old code. This ships in 1.19.2 alongside the CEL work, and only there. The legacy engine is on its way out, so the effort belongs in the engine replacing it. What this does not fix The engine still pays one JSON round-trip of the admitted object per request, to preserve the raw, un-normalized parse that request.object has always exposed. Evaluating against the typed object, or a cheaper representation, would remove even that — but it would change what policies see, so it needs its own design. Mutating policies thread full objects between policies rather than propagating a patch diff. A patch-only model is a substantially larger redesign and is not implemented. Tail latency under sustained load on a single replica is not addressed by any of this, and we have not re-measured it since. If you have seen Kyverno’s p95 swing widely between runs at high load, that is a separate problem and it is still open. Limitations Single machine. Everything here reproduces the relationship between configurations, not the absolute numbers you would see on a 32-core server. Most of this is a Go benchmark. The allocation and timing figures come from benchmarks driving the real engine loop, and the profiles come from those benchmark runs. They isolate the engine cleanly, and they exclude network, serialization at the webhook boundary, and etcd. The engine comparison uses loopback, so the webhook network hop is excluded, and dry-run, so the etcd write is excluded. The native side runs Kyverno’s generated policies, which is a faithful same-policy comparison rather than a hand-tuned native policy set. Side controllers were disabled in these runs. Only the admission controller was active. Reproduce it The harness is in the Kyverno repository under docs/perf-testing/: the version ladder, the pinned Pod Security Standards policy set, the k6 scripts, and the cluster setup. The engine benchmarks live beside the code they measure, in pkg/cel/policies/vpol/engine and pkg/engine/context. If you benchmark Kyverno and get a result you do not like, please publish it — with the method, the caveats, and the per-trial numbers. Conclusion Our mission at Kyverno is to be the best policy engine for Kubernetes and beyond. Admission control is a critical process in Kubernetes clusters, and a slow or misconfigured controller can impact cluster operations. Thanks to our community, we have fixed performance issues and added more tests. For future releases, we will be looking at improving concurrency and further optimization. Thanks to Mustafa Erdinç, whose comparison of different Kubernetes policy engines motivated this work. title: [Pulumi] Introducing Pulumi Delivery: your release pipeline as code
summary: Coding agents have made writing software faster than shipping it. The bottleneck is now everything after the code: release pipelines full of bespoke scripts, console steps, and hand-run promotions that slow teams down and don’t scale. Today, we’re introducing Pulumi Delivery, available in public preview. With Delivery, you define how a change moves from development through staging to production in the same languages you already use for infrastructure: TypeScript, Python, Go, HCL, YAML, and more. Your pipeline becomes a Pulumi program, so it gets the same policies and review process as the rest of your infrastructure, whether a person or an agent wrote the change. The new bottleneck Most applications span many infrastructure stacks. For example, your service may have separate stacks per environment for its networking layer, database, and application code, and they need to be deployed in the correct order. Today, that ordering and the rest of your delivery logic live in standalone pipeline files and manual console steps. Those tools run separately from your infrastructure, your secrets, and your policies, so the rules you enforce on a stack often don’t apply to the pipeline that deploys it. Reusing logic across services usually means copying YAML, and testing a pipeline usually means running it and watching. Agents make that gap wider. They’re fluent in code, but the context needed to promote a release is scattered across consoles and config files they can’t see or access. Delivery puts your release pipeline in the same code your agents already work in, so you can ship as fast as they write. Your delivery pipeline, as code A Delivery pipeline is a Pulumi program. In it, you declare the repositories you deploy from, the stages a release moves through, the stacks each stage updates, and the gates that hold a release. Pulumi Cloud then runs each release through those stages in order. Delivery pins the release to that commit, so the code that passed in staging is exactly the code that reaches prod. Because a pipeline is a real program, you can express common patterns like promotion logic, canary rollouts, blue-green deployments, and multi-region sequencing as composable code. Write a rollout pattern once as a function, reuse it across services, and test it like any other code. One pipeline for all your stacks Getting the order right is what makes a release safe, and the more stacks you have, the harder it is to get right. Delivery uses what Pulumi already knows about your infrastructure to work out the order for you. When your app stack depends on a value from your network stack, such as a subnet ID, Delivery updates the network first and the app second, without you writing that order down anywhere. Stacks that don’t depend on each other update at the same time. You still set the big steps, such as dev, staging, and prod, yourself, and you can order individual stacks by hand when you need to. Gate releases with AI risk review Approval gates work well until the number of changes outgrows the number of people available to review them. With Delivery, you can add an AI reviewer as a gate. It assesses each change’s risk and either promotes the change or escalates it to a human for review. You can also gate releases on decision models such as TypeSafe’s Jev, which return a calibrated risk score. Your pipeline compares that score against a threshold you set, so routine changes move on their own and the risky ones wait for a person. You decide where that line sits, and you can move it as you build trust in the results. Turn production signals into reviewed fixes Delivery can also react to the observability tools you already have, including PagerDuty, Honeycomb, Sentry, and Datadog. When a signal points to a problem in production, an agent can prepare a fix and open a pull request under your policies. That fix then moves through the same pipeline as any other change, with the same gates at every stage. Agents get a fast path to production that’s also the governed one. title: [Microsoft Azure] Microsoft and Oracle bring agentic AI into flow of enterprise work
summary: This blog is co-authored by Arpan Shah, SVP of Oracle Databases and Muneer Mirza, VP of Multicloud at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). Today at Microsoft Ignite, we’re bringing agentic AI into the flow of enterprise work. Our new integrations let AI agents reason across Oracle’s business-critical data—from finance and supply chain to HR and customer operations—and the work context Microsoft Work IQ understands across meetings, email, documents, and Teams. Customers can access this combined intelligence through Excel, Teams, and Microsoft Copilot. Built on Oracle AI Database@Azure, the integrations help businesses turn trusted enterprise data into insights and actions, with the choice, security, and performance mission-critical workloads demand. Learn more about Oracle on Azure With Oracle AI Database@Azure, Oracle and Microsoft have helped customers modernize critical workloads to improve application performance and unlock more value from their enterprise data, by bringing databases closer to applications and connecting enterprise data with Microsoft AI. Oracle AI Database@Azure now spans 33 Azure regions, more than on any other hyperscaler, delivering the performance and flexibility customers need. At Oracle AI World 2026, we announced new capabilities for Oracle AI Database@Azure including FedRAMP Class D certification coming soon for US Government and public-sector workloads, and Proximity Placement Groups (PPGs) that enable customers to place their database closer to applications—resulting in approximately 50% lower VM-to-Exadata network round-trip latency than deployments without PPG alignment. Now, at Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re building on that momentum. For IT operations: Monitoring and trust at every layer Today, we’re announcing limited preview of Azure Workload Center for Oracle, bringing each workload’s architecture, resources, and dependencies together through a construct called a Workload Virtual Instance (WVI). This significantly reduces the complexity and resources required to manage solutions at the individual component level. Integrations across the Workload Virtual Instance, Azure Monitor Health Models, and the Microsoft Azure Copilot Run Oracle agent connect monitoring signals across application, database, and infrastructure layers. This operational visibility is complemented by agent access controls: Oracle AI Database@Azure supports Microsoft Entra authentication and Oracle Deep Data Security, helping agents stay within users’ existing permissions while database calls run through the managed model context protocol (MCP) server and activity remains auditable across your Oracle database estate. For example, after business users report poor performance from an order processing application, an admin must quickly diagnose and fix the problem. The admin signs in with their existing Microsoft Entra identity and uses Azure Workload Center for Oracle to get a unified view of workload health including signals across the infrastructure, database, and application layers while Copilot provides a summary highlighting where to focus. The admin uses a natural-language prompt to initiate a coordinated investigation involving multiple agents, each with Oracle data access limited by their identify profile. Database calls from the agents run through the managed MCP server, and every action is captured for audit. Working together, the agents synthesize their findings into a single operational conclusion for the admin. For end users: Oracle data in the flow of work Business users need insights from Oracle data, but they often need assistance from someone more technical to extract, format, and deliver it. The new Oracle AI Database plug-in for Excel, available today, lets users connect Excel directly to Oracle Database, pull trusted data into the worksheet, and reason over it with Copilot without leaving the spreadsheet. No export, no manual preparation, no ticket to IT. Together, Microsoft and Oracle are bringing intelligence to the workflows that run the business: giving analysts, planners and controllers the power to understand margin changes, analyze shifts in demand, resolve reconciliation issues, and act on supply chain disruptions. Copilot analyzes Oracle transaction data and enriches it with context from Work IQ, drawn from meetings, email, documents and Teams, to identify exceptions, draft an explanation, and prepare a governed action plan for review. Rather than another dashboard, or disconnected chatbot, this is AI in the flow of work, grounded in systems of record maintained in Oracle AI Database. For developers: Build trusted agents quickly, from prototype to production Pilots are easy; production is hard. Real processes span multiple data sources, call for several specialized agents, and demand answers a business can stand behind. Developers can build agents that connect to Oracle AI Database using Microsoft Foundry with Managed Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and A2A protocol. MCP servers enable governed access from Azure agents to Oracle AI Database, whether it runs in Oracle Cloud Infrastructure or as Oracle AI Database@Azure, through approved SQL and PL/SQL operations, tools, and predefined reports. Application roles determine which tools each user or group can use, so agents never reach beyond what IT has sanctioned, and AI comes to the data rather than the data being copied out to AI. These integrations make Oracle AI Database a first-class source of knowledge, memory, and data for agents built in Microsoft Foundry. For example, a developer builds a sales intelligence application involving an agent retrieving account and order data from Oracle AI Database through MCP, a product agent identifying cross-sell opportunities, and a finance agent weighing in on account health. Through coordinated activity across these agents, the sales intelligence team receives a concise sales brief through an API. In another scenario, a customer service agent, grounded through Foundry IQ, can answer questions about a policy or an account with supporting citations, and recall the customer history from Oracle-backed memory, retrieve similar past interactions, and responds with context. title: [Microsoft Azure] Azure Cobalt 200 VMs now available, proven on real workloads and built for the agentic era
summary: Today at Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re announcing the general availability of Azure Cobalt 200-based virtual machines (VMs). Cobalt 200 VMs deliver up to 50% better performance than Cobalt 100 and are now available in 14 regions, expanding to 23 regions by the end of 2026. Built for cloud-native, data-intensive, and agentic AI workloads, Cobalt 200 VMs will represent a significant share of new Azure Compute capacity beginning in 2027. Explore Cobalt 200 VM sizes and deployment guidance For customers like Amadeus, Databricks, InMobi, OpenAI, and Snowflake, Cobalt 200 VMs deliver improved performance and efficiency over Cobalt 100 VMs. As a result, customers can deliver faster search results, more responsive database queries, and run their services at higher utilization with fewer cores. Cobalt 200’s performance and efficiency gains reflect our systems approach to infrastructure design, which co-optimizes silicon, software, networking, power, and rack infrastructure. Cobalt 200 VMs are also designed for agentic AI workflows, including agent sandboxes, file search, code compilation, and tool execution, where higher per-core performance can help reduce latency. As customer need for high-performance and low-latency compute increases, we’re adding new virtual machine types to bring the price-performance benefits of Cobalt to additional workloads: Mpsv4 for high memory workloads. Lpsv5 for workloads needing fast access to large datasets. With Microsoft Azure Boost included in every Cobalt 200 VM, customers get the latest accelerated network and remote storage performance in Microsoft Azure. Proven on critical customer workloads Our benchmarking for Cobalt 200 VMs showed significant performance increases for a wide variety of workloads. We observed up to 1.5 times increased performance for web serving workloads, up to 1.6 times for Java-based workloads, up to 1.5 times for AI agent tool execution workloads, and 1.9 times for database workloads over Cobalt 100. We’ve seen these results translate into real-world improvements as our customers bring Cobalt 200 VMs to their own workloads. See what customers are saying about Cobalt 200 VMs Cobalt has helped us sustain ChatGPT’s growth. Cobalt 100 gave us more CPU capacity when we needed it. By the time we tested Cobalt 200, our services already ran on ARM, so we could compare the same ChatGPT workloads on both generations. We saw higher throughput and lower latency on Cobalt 200. That means we can serve more users with the same number of cores, and they spend less time waiting for ChatGPT to start responding. —Vadim Filanovsky, Member of Technical Staff, OpenAI Genie, the data-smart AI coworker, puts answers in front of business users in plain language, and those answers depend on fast, efficient compute underneath. Azure Cobalt helps us deliver that. Azure Databricks serverless compute on Cobalt starts faster and runs more efficiently, so customers spend less time waiting and more time acting on their data. Cobalt 200 raises the bar again, and as we bring more of Azure Databricks onto it, Genie questions, SQL queries, and data pipelines get faster. —Vinod Marur, SVP Engineering, Databricks Snowflake has grown with Arm on Azure, from the first Arm-based v5 VMs to Cobalt 100 and now Cobalt 200. Each generation has brought real performance and efficiency gains for our workloads, and those gains help us give our customers an even better experience. We’re proud to partner with Microsoft on what comes next for Cobalt and excited to see Cobalt 200 reach general availability. —Murray Stokely, Distinguished Engineer, Snowflake Performance at scale is at the heart of how Amadeus serves the travel industry. In our benchmark lab, Azure Cobalt 200 improved flight search throughput by more than 30% compared with Cobalt 100, a performance gain that exceeded our expectations. —Luc Choubert, VP Engineering, Amadeus We tested our ad-serving workloads on Cobalt 200 and saw clear performance and efficiency improvements. In addition to traditional workload patterns, we run high-throughput local neural network inference using SIMD, with each 32-core machine processing approximately 50,000 inferences per second. At the scale of a large fleet, these per-machine efficiency gains compound significantly, making Cobalt 200 particularly compelling for our workloads. —Sudheer Bhat, Principal Engineer, InMobi Partner endorsements Microsoft’s continued investment in Cobalt demonstrates the value of building cloud infrastructure on Arm. Our collaboration on Cobalt 200 brings together Arm Neoverse CSS V3 and Microsoft’s custom silicon innovation to deliver the high performance and efficiency needed for everything from enterprise applications to agentic AI. —Mohamed Awad, EVP, Cloud AI, Arm Cobalt 200 VMs bring the performance and efficiency that agentic AI and data workloads need in production. Ubuntu supports Arm as a first-class architecture, so teams deploy Ubuntu on Cobalt 200 VMs the way they already do across Azure. Ubuntu Pro keeps those systems patched and supported for the long term. On Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, that includes Kernel Livepatch, which applies high and critical kernel fixes on Arm-based VMs without a reboot. —Cindy Goldberg, VP, Cloud and Silicon Partnerships, Canonical Improving efficiency at Microsoft scale Microsoft products and services, including Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure DevOps, Azure SQL, Microsoft 365, XBOX, and more, run on Cobalt VMs for increased performance, improved efficiency, and cost savings at scale. Accelerating cloud database workloads Cobalt 200 was designed to deliver high-performance for database workloads, and at Microsoft Build 2026, we announced the availability of Azure Database for PostgreSQL on Cobalt 200. Cobalt 200 VMs provide scalable performance, memory capacity, and local storage needed to accelerate Azure Database for PostgreSQL. Advancing custom silicon development Microsoft’s silicon engineers run EDA workloads for design verification, physical implementation, and sign-off, and they benchmarked many of those workloads on Cobalt 200 VMs. The team reported increased performance and efficiency with Cobalt 200, with performance between 1.3 and 4.15 times over Cobalt 100. The increased performance allows the team to run more test cases in the same amount of time, supporting the development of more advanced Maia and Cobalt silicon. Speeding up developer workflows Every second counts when developers are waiting on a build. Cobalt 200 VMs allow GitHub Actions larger Arm runners to finish jobs noticeably faster than on Cobalt 100. Across the millions of workflows run every day, those gains add up to faster feedback for developers and more efficient use of compute. Gaming XBOX evaluated Cobalt 200 VMs on its web service and caching layer, the behind-the-scenes building blocks that help players sign in, see what their friends are playing and jump into games more quickly. Running natively on Arm, XBOX achieved improved performance and efficiency compared to their current infrastructure, a jump that matters in gaming for delivering fast and reliable gameplay. Scaling media processing The media processing service running video for Microsoft Teams observed 1.65 times the performance on Cobalt 200 compared with Cobalt 100, allowing them to further optimize their capacity needs to serve customers. Testing also showed linear scaling across Cobalt 200 physical cores, with vCPU utilization reaching up to 90% while serving traffic. Compute designed for agents, powered by custom systems Modern AI applications have evolved from simple inference-based chat interfaces to complex reasoning and agentic systems requiring high-performance compute infrastructure paired with AI acceleration. Cobalt 200 is optimized from the lowest levels of the silicon to the overall rack and system architecture for the demands of agentic compute. Azure Cobalt 200 server board At the center of every Cobalt 200 VM is the Cobalt 200 system-on-chip (SoC). Built on TSMC’s advanced 3nm process technology to deliver optimal performance and efficiency, the Cobalt 200 SoC brings together 132 Arm Neoverse V3 cores, with a multi-chipset architecture, and advanced packaging. Compute: Each vCPU is a full physical core, with 3MB of private L2 cache, and 192 MB of system-level cache, helping provide consistent performance under load while keeping recently accessed data close to the core. Memory: Cobalt 200 features a custom memory controller with 12 channels of DDR5 and enables memory encryption by default with negligible latency. Networking and storage: Cobalt 200 VMs include the latest version of Azure Boost, moving networking and storage processing off the host, delivering up to 15% higher network bandwidth, 20% higher remote storage IOPS, and 10% higher remote storage throughput compared with Cobalt 100. Security: Every Cobalt 200 server includes the Azure Integrated HSM which protects the server hardware from unauthorized intrusion and enables protected encryption key storage for hosted workloads. Acceleration: Integrated compression and cryptography accelerators enable Microsoft workloads to reduce CPU consumption by offloading common tasks to specialized low-power silicon. On-chip accelerators will help reduce Azure SQL backup times by up to 2.5 times while minimizing disruption to the live workload. Expanding choice and control Predictable performance or peak performance. Cobalt 200 VMs support two processor modes. Deterministic Mode runs cores at a consistent 3.2 GHz. Opportunistic Mode can boost cores up to 3.6 GHz when power and thermal headroom allow—delivering up to 12% more performance at the expense of some frequency variability. Different customers have different needs. Deterministic Mode suits distributed data and analytics clusters which run at the pace of their slowest node, and services with tight performance targets. Opportunistic Mode suits web and API services, transaction processing, and media workloads, where speed matters more than consistency. Use the ProcessorMode setting to choose deterministic or opportunistic mode when you create a VM or later through the Azure portal, Microsoft Azure CLI, PowerShell, or Azure Resource Manager and Biceptemplates. title: [Engineering at Meta] Intelligent Delivery: Making Every Unit of Compute Serve Better Ads
summary: Ads ranking models are growing toward LLM scale faster than the hardware to run them can keep up. An extra unit of compute has more impact on some ad requests, models, and chips than on others. The challenge is deciding where to allocate it to get the best outcome for the entire system. We built Intelligent Delivery, an ML-driven system that allocates resources across the serving stack toward the system-wide optimum. It has delivered ~10% incremental ranking performance on top of model and system advancements since 2017. We’re sharing a few of Intelligent Delivery’s capabilities: how we build ML models to predict the marginal utility of compute, multi-layered mechanisms to move resources across the system, and how we increasingly leverage agentic AI to continuously detect and respond to system shifts. As frontier ads ranking systems advance toward larger models, broader candidate sets, and richer delivery architectures, they also place greater demands on serving efficiency. Compute resources do not scale at the rate that models and system complexity do. The challenge is not just how to build more powerful models, but how to operate them efficiently across a heterogeneous system, with finite serving capacity, and under a tight latency budget. We recently shared how we put idle inference capacity to work. This post covers how we decide where each unit of compute goes to achieve globally optimal system efficiency. Intelligent Delivery is our approach to the problem, and it has contributed an additional ~10% improvement in ads ranking performance on top of model and system advancements across major surfaces, from 2017 through the first half of 2026. It introduces an ML-driven, increasingly AI-operated adaptive optimization layer that continuously directs resources toward the requests, models, hardware fleets, and ranking stages with the highest marginal utility. This helps us run advanced ads ranking models efficiently in production, getting more out of every unit of compute to serve better ads for people who use our apps and services. The Goal and What Makes It Difficult One of our goals is to create a delivery system that continuously converges on its global optimum, regardless of how user behavior changes, models evolve, and the serving stack grows more complex. Three fundamental properties of ads delivery systems make this challenging: The marginal impact of compute is highly heterogeneous and context-dependent: The same additional unit of compute can generate very different returns depending on the product surface, user intent, candidate quality, and system state. Request-aware signals alone are not sufficient; allocating well means estimating, for every request, the return on every available tunable system parameter, where each knob behaves differently at each stage of the funnel. We need to produce a per-request result calculation across a vast decision space within milliseconds. Local optimality does not translate to global optimality: Result estimation is just the start; the serving stack must also be dynamically controllable. Ads delivery spans multi-stage ranking, hundreds of models, generations of hardware, and many data centers. Resources cannot be shifted freely and reliably across these boundaries without adaptive controls that account for complex dependencies throughout the stack. The global optimum is a moving target: The optimization landscape is continuously shifting. Every new model, hardware generation, or new architecture changes the landscape and can invalidate previously optimal allocation decisions. The system needs to adapt quickly enough to retain its optimality. Intelligent Delivery includes three capabilities, each designed to address one of these fundamental system challenges. Capabilities of Intelligent Delivery 1. Request Understanding: A Shared ML Intelligence Layer for Compute Some ad requests benefit more from additional computation than others. Initially, we captured these differences through coarse segments: Requests were grouped by attributes such as surface, context, and ad creative representation, with engineers creating policies to allocate resources for each group. This approach delivered improvements but did not scale. Every new signal multiplied the rules, making the effort unsustainable, and independent segments could not capture the nonlinear interactions among thousands of signals, which limited accuracy. We achieved about a 20% improvement in identifying the highest-impact ad requests in offline benchmarks on major surfaces, relative to our previous production model, after reframing this into two ML problems: Which ad requests are most likely to benefit from additional compute? And how will different resource settings affect their outcomes and serving performance? A side-by-side comparison of static rule-based segmentation, where every request in a bucket gets the same compute, and signal-driven decisions, where an ML-driven predictor sets compute for each request. To answer the first question, we built the Resource Core Model, deep learning models with 6B sparse parameters and 20M dense parameters that run once before candidate retrieval and are shared across the delivery funnel. Learned embeddings and deep feature interactions capture nuanced request patterns that manually defined segments cannot. We then fine-tune the Resource Core Model into a set of specialized models, each generating incremental signals about outcome, compute consumption, and latency impact. Together this forms a shared ML intelligence layer for resource allocation: The Resource Core Model understands each request and its serving behavior, while individual mechanisms determine how to translate those predictions into actions. An architecture diagram of the Resource Core Model, showing how dense and sparse request features pass through stacked interaction layers to predict each request’s outcome, compute consumption, and latency impact. 2. Allocation Mechanisms: A Hierarchy of Decision Engines Ads serving runs on a globally distributed, heterogeneous fleet with many data center regions, several hardware generations, and millions of hosts, all shared by a multi-tier serving stack. A single allocation mechanism cannot control the complex resource distribution end to end. So we decomposed the problem into a hierarchy of layers and built a dedicated decision engine for each. The easiest way to see the hierarchy is to follow a single request through it. Someone opens their feed. An ad request is created, and over the next few hundred milliseconds it passes through a chain of resource allocation decisions. This leads us to three important questions and answers. Which region serves it? Traffic and capacity are not colocated, and each region carries a different hardware mix and a different amount of headroom — so the same unit of compute is more efficient in some places than in others. We built real-time infrastructure to dynamically shift traffic between regions in a cycle of minutes, driving toward the point where every region achieves the same level of efficiency on its marginal unit of capacity. What hardware does it land on? Our fleet spans CPUs from Intel, AMD, and Arm and accelerators from NVIDIA, AMD, and our own Meta Training and Inference Accelerator (MTIA), across several generations of each. The hard part isn’t the variety; it’s that capacity isn’t interchangeable. Our stages are bound by different resources — retrieval by memory capacity, ranking by compute, and model inference by accelerator throughput — so there is no single fastest SKU, only a best match per workload. We benchmark measured efficiency for every workload-SKU pair, then solve the assignment so that scarce hardware goes to the workloads that convert it into the most useful work. Inside the host, how much of this machine does the request get? Concurrent requests differ in latency budget and impact, under a hard tail-latency SLO. We predict each request’s expected outcome and its compute and latency cost in real time using our advanced deep learning models, and solve a constrained optimization that maximizes impact delivered within the host’s latency budget — as the host load increases, the performance trade-off rises and resource-intensive low-impact work is trimmed first. Enforcing those decisions takes control across the whole stack, so the framework spans from kernel-level scheduler up to application-level thread pools. A three-step flowchart following one ad request through the decision hierarchy: which region serves it, which hardware it runs on, and how much of the host it gets. These three steps are just a subset of the allocation decisions we make during a request’s lifecycle. Following this, we optimize the number of ads to rank for each request in each ranking stage, what ad candidates enter the pool, and much more. These allocation decisions are tightly coupled, so a resource change in any one of them ripples across the whole system. Shifting traffic between regions changes per-host load, which drives the feedback controller that sets how much work each request gets. We validate these changes in an end-to-end, closed-loop hardware testing environment to make sure we are optimizing for the global optimum instead of a local optimum. 3. Optimization Loop: Self-Optimizing Serving with Agentic AI As our ad system advances, productionizing a new model, a new mechanism, or new hardware into the system requires a lot of effort to achieve seamless integration. We can’t brute-force every single configuration across millions of tunable dimensions built in our system for a new change. That would require too much time and far more hardware resources than we have. We relied heavily on human expertise and engineers’ prior knowledge to identify promising configurations. But this approach didn’t scale, because every new model, mechanism, and hardware generation expanded the search space faster than engineers could explore it. We tried automating this with a constrained optimization approach, which delivered improvements but remained inflexible and slow. We found that it lacked the ability to generalize (it could only cover a few key knobs) and couldn’t effectively incorporate human intuition from prior experience. Instead of doing a blind search, AI agents continuously monitor the entire system landscape, identifying changes and inefficiencies to address. In a long context window, an agent reads mechanism source code, design documents, and a decade of experiment logs and narrows that to a handful of changes worth testing. Engineers review and approve the final change before it ships. Today, agents can already propose well-reasoned changes and design and run rigorous experiments. In the first half of 2026, agents contributed to about 20% of Intelligent Delivery optimizations. On our most automated mechanism, they now contribute to about 80% of the engineering effort, from understanding the system landscape and forming hypotheses to running experiments and converging on the final change. This shortens the optimization loop from months to weeks while keeping people firmly in control. And it steadily captures the expertise engineers have built over the years. A loop diagram of the AI-driven optimization cycle, where agents collect data, propose changes, and run experiments, with an engineer approving every change and a shared knowledge base feeding each step. The Next Frontiers for Intelligent Delivery End-to-end real-time optimization: Today, understanding a request and deciding how to serve it are still two separate steps. We’re building toward fusing them into a single model that reads a request and serves it in real time, without months of experiments. There’s established work in varying compute per request with learning-based methods. However, doing it jointly across every serving stage at once — under shifting traffic, hard capacity limits, and tight inter-stage dependencies — is the part that’s still open, and it’s what we’re pushing on. Serving state-of-the-art models on GPUs: Large ranking models, like Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM), are growing toward LLM scale and increasingly run on GPUs, which opens a different optimization space. GPU capacity doesn’t divide the way CPU time does — it comes in whole, fixed blocks, and throughput, batching, and memory all behave differently. The levers we built for a CPU world have to be reimagined, and much of our work now goes into understanding those mechanisms and turning them into new levers. The more useful work we get out of each accelerator, the more people we can serve with strong models under the same capacity. title: [HashiCorp] From exposed secrets to managed credentials: Reducing credential risk across the application lifecycle
summary: A recent software supply chain attack affecting tens of thousands of GitHub repositories highlights a security problem that is easy to underestimate: a credential does not stop being exposed simply because it has been deleted from the latest version of the code. Researchers uncovered a campaign in which attackers inserted a malicious GitHub Actions workflow into repositories they had permission to modify. Designed to look like a routine security audit, the workflow instead searched for and exfiltrated credentials. It targeted secrets available to GitHub Actions, but also searched repository files and complete Git history for credentials associated with cloud providers and AI services. That meant credentials developers had previously committed and later removed could still be discovered. The incident is another reminder that responding to exposed credentials requires more than cleaning up source code. Organizations need to understand where credentials have been exposed, remediate those credentials and ultimately improve how they are managed. HCP Vault Radar and HashiCorp Vault can help teams address different parts of that lifecycle, moving from discovering exposed secrets to bringing credentials under centralized management. A deleted secret can still be an exposed secret Accidentally committing a credential is not an unusual scenario in software development. An API key gets added to a configuration file while testing an integration, a cloud credential helps get a prototype running, or a token is placed into a workflow to solve an immediate problem. A developer may eventually identify the mistake and remove the credential, leaving the current version of the application looking clean. But removing the plaintext value does not necessarily remediate the underlying credential. The secret can remain in Git history, the original credential may still be active, and copies may exist in other places across the development lifecycle. In this attack, that distinction was particularly important because the malicious workflow specifically searched historical repository content for credentials. HCP Vault Radar helps teams find exposed and unmanaged secrets across development environments, including credentials that persist in Git history. That visibility can help security teams understand where credential exposure exists and prioritize remediation, particularly when a secret may no longer appear in the latest version of the repository. Finding the exposure, however, does not address the credential itself. If a discovered credential remains active, teams still need to investigate the exposure and revoke or rotate the credential with the relevant provider. Move from discovery to remediation Once the exposed credential has been addressed, teams also need to consider how the replacement credential will be managed. Generating a new credential and putting it back into source code or another configuration file may resolve the immediate exposure, but it recreates the same underlying problem. This is where Vault complements the discovery capabilities of Vault Radar. Vault provides a centralized way to secure credentials and control how applications access them. Instead of embedding a replacement credential in source code, teams can bring the credential under management in Vault and update the application, agent, or workload to retrieve it when needed. The application can still get the credential where it needs it without putting the credential back into source code. Where supported, organizations can take that model further by using dynamic, short-lived credentials instead of relying on long-lived static credentials. A long-lived credential discovered in an old commit could remain useful to an attacker until someone identifies the exposure and revokes it. Short-lived credentials reduce that window because they are created when needed and expire after a defined period. Not every application or third-party service supports dynamic credentials, so static credentials will continue to be part of many environments. Those credentials still benefit from centralized management, controlled access and rotation rather than being distributed throughout source code and development workflows. Together, Vault Radar and Vault create a more complete path from credential exposure to credential management. Radar goes beyond scanning source code by helping teams discover exposed and unmanaged secrets across the broader development ecosystem and providing the context needed to investigate and prioritize findings. Vault then provides the management layer for securing those credentials, controlling access and reducing reliance on long-lived credentials where possible. The combination helps teams move beyond finding exposed secrets toward reducing the unmanaged credentials that created the risk in the first place. Credential exposure extends beyond source code Git repositories are also only one place credentials can escape. The same credential can move across the software development lifecycle as teams build, test and troubleshoot applications, appearing in tickets, documentation, collaboration systems, cloud storage, CI/CD logs and artifacts, or other development environments. Even after the original secret is removed from source code, copies can remain across the tools and systems developers use every day. That makes broader visibility important when responding to an exposed secret. Instead of treating a finding as an isolated string in a single repository, security teams need to understand where else that credential may have spread and the context surrounding the exposure. Vault Radar extends secret discovery across supported developer and collaboration environments, cloud infrastructure and software artifacts, helping teams identify credential exposure beyond source code. Combined with Vault, teams can use that visibility not only to remediate individual findings, but also to bring exposed credentials back under a more consistent management model. From exposed secrets to managed credentials The lesson from this latest attack is not that better secrets management can prevent every software supply chain compromise. The attack began with malicious access to repositories and involved a broader compromise of the software development process. But it also shows how exposed credentials can increase the impact of an attack once an attacker gets inside. That makes credential security an important part of reducing the potential blast radius. Teams need a way to find credentials that have escaped, remediate the immediate exposure and improve how those credentials are managed going forward. Vault Radar helps identify exposed and unmanaged secrets so teams can understand where credential risk exists. Vault provides the management layer for securing credentials, controlling access, rotating secrets and, where supported, replacing long-lived credentials with dynamic, short-lived access. The goal is not simply to remove a secret from a repository. It is to reduce the number of unmanaged credentials available to steal and establish a lifecycle for keeping credentials secure after they are discovered. Deleting the secret may clean up the code. Remediating the credential and changing how it is managed addresses the risk. Get started Finding an exposed secret is only the first step. Learn how organizations can build a more resilient approach to credential risk, from identifying exposures to improving how credentials are managed across the application lifecycle, in the credential risk whitepaper. Explore Vault Radar to uncover unmanaged and exposed secrets across development workflows, and HCP Vault Dedicated to bring credentials under centralized secrets management and reduce reliance on long-lived credentials where possible.
